shortDescription: Electric vehicles are displacing five times as much oil as they did five years ago, but Central and Eastern Europe, which is emerging as a major manufacturing hub for the industry, remains one of the slowest regions in Europe to adopt them.Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) now displace around 1.2mn…

children: Electric vehicles are displacing five times as much oil as they did five years ago, but Central and Eastern Europe, which is emerging as a major manufacturing hub for the industry, remains one of the slowest regions in Europe to adopt them.

Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) now displace around 1.2mn barrels of oil per day, equivalent to 1.2% of global consumption, up from 215,000 bpd in 2021, according to an analysis published by Brussels-based campaign group Transport & Environment (T&E). The findings come five years after the COP26 climate summit in Glasgow.

BEVs account for just 4.2% of the global car fleet but around a quarter of new vehicle sales, compared with 6.6% five years ago. Their adoption avoids more than 200mn tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions annually. Electric buses and trucks displace up to another 320,000 bpd of oil, T&E estimates.

On current policies, electric cars could displace around 5.8mn bpd by 2034, approximately equivalent to the oil supply lost during this year's crisis, when the Iran war disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and depleted global stocks.

'Electric vehicles are the single most effective way of cutting oil demand. Right now the only winners in our oil addiction are fossil fuel giants and petrostates,' said Antony Froggatt, senior director at T&E.
'Places with near 100% sales of EVs like Norway, Denmark and Hong Kong have effectively insulated themselves from future shocks,' he added.

Central and Eastern Europe, however, is struggling to replicate that transition. Battery electric cars accounted for 24% of new registrations across Europe in the first nine months of 2026, but only 5% in Poland, the region's largest car market, and 4% in Croatia, according to the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT).

The contrast is striking because the region is simultaneously becoming one of Europe's most important centres for electric vehicle and battery production. BMW, Mercedes-Benz and BYD are establishing major manufacturing operations in Hungary, CATL is building its largest battery factory outside China there, while Volvo is preparing to start production at a new plant in Slovakia.

The region therefore faces a double exposure to the transition: it is increasingly dependent on manufacturing electric vehicles for western European consumers while its own motorists remain heavily reliant on imported oil.
A widening gap with western Europe

Slovenia is the regional frontrunner, with battery electric vehicles accounting for 21% of new registrations in January-September, close to the European average. Latvia followed with 11%, Bulgaria and Hungary with 10%, Romania and Estonia with 8%, and Czechia and Slovakia with 7%, ICCT data show.

Conventional combustion engines remain dominant in several markets. In Czechia, home to Skoda, they accounted for 62% of new car registrations, compared with 28% across Europe. The share was 58% in Croatia and 52% in Slovakia.

Poland was the only European market where the share of battery electric vehicles declined, falling by one percentage point despite a 10% increase in overall registrations. BEV registrations dropped 3% to just under 25,000, while plug-in hybrid sales almost doubled and full and mild hybrids together accounted for more than half the market.
Fully electric vehicles represented 6.1% of Polish passenger car registrations in September, down from 8.9% a year earlier, according to automotive research firm Samar.
Elsewhere, however, sales are expanding rapidly from a low base. BEV registrations more than doubled in Slovenia, Bulgaria and Croatia during the first nine months of the year.

In Romania, where the overall car market contracted by 10.1% in January-October, electric vehicle registrations increased 45.6% to 9,384, according to carmakers' association ACAROM. Chinese manufacturer BYD sold 4,969 vehicles, making it the country's sixth-largest car brand.
BYD also became Hungary's leading seller of new energy vehicles in 2025, while electric registrations in Slovenia more than doubled last year to reach 11% of new car sales.
Higher fuel costs strengthen the case for electrification

The economic argument for switching is becoming more compelling as motorists face higher fuel prices. EU fuel prices were 31.4% higher in September than a year earlier, with Bulgaria recording the sharpest increase, at 42.2%, followed by Estonia and Lithuania, according to Eurostat.
Hungary's government opted for targeted support rather than reinstating a general fuel price cap, offering HUF20,000 (€55) in compensation to owners of smaller diesel cars.

The oil shock had cost EU road users an estimated €53bn by early October, including €40bn spent on diesel, T&E calculated in a separate report. Charging an electric vehicle at home costs roughly half as much as running a petrol or diesel car, the organisation said.
Nearly 8mn electric vehicles on EU roads avoided 46mn barrels of oil consumption in 2025, equivalent to €2.9bn at prevailing prices, according to the report.

The issue is particularly sensitive in Hungary, which remains heavily dependent on Russian crude. Russia supplied more than 90% of Hungarian oil imports in 2025. A US waiver covering purchases of Russian crude by Hungarian refiner MOL through the Druzhba pipeline is due to expire on November 21, months before the company expects to be able to operate its Hungarian refinery and Slovakia's Slovnaft plant fully on seaborne supplies routed through Croatia.
The region becomes Europe's EV assembly line
Hungary has moved furthest in attracting investment in electric vehicle manufacturing.

BMW's €2bn plant in Debrecen, its first factory dedicated to producing vehicles based on the Neue Klasse platform, had manufactured more than 50,000 iX3 vehicles by October. Production is running around the clock on three shifts, with the iX4 also being added to the line.

Mercedes-Benz began manufacturing its electric C-Class at Kecskemet in July following a €1bn investment. The facility is now the German manufacturer's largest European plant, with annual capacity of around 350,000 vehicles.
BYD plans to begin serial production at its €5bn Szeged factory in the fourth quarter, initially targeting annual capacity of around 150,000 vehicles, with the potential to double output to 300,000.

Chinese battery manufacturer CATL began trial production of battery cells at its €7.3bn Debrecen facility on September 22, later than its previously announced spring target. The growing contribution of new automotive investments was already visible in Hungary's industrial statistics, with output rising 8.2% year on year in September. Erste Bank chief analyst Orsolya Nyeste attributed the increase partly to production at BMW's Debrecen and Mercedes-Benz's Kecskemet plants.

The rapid expansion has also raised environmental concerns. Debrecen's mayor ordered Chinese battery separator manufacturer Semcorp to leave the city in July after heavy metals were detected in groundwater near its factory.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is preparing to establish a new environmental authority from January 1, with fines of up to HUF5bn (€13.7mn) for the most serious violations. Hungary has become the world's fourth-largest electric vehicle battery producer, with more than 10,000 people employed in the sector.

Slovakia is also positioning itself as a manufacturing centre. Volvo has started test production at its new electric vehicle factory in Valaliky near Kosice, which is designed to produce up to 250,000 cars annually once serial manufacturing begins in 2027.

Volkswagen's battery subsidiary PowerCo is taking a 49% stake in a 20 GWh lithium iron phosphate battery plant under construction at Surany. The project is being developed by Gotion InoBat Batteries, a joint venture between China's Gotion High-Tech and Slovakia's InoBat.

In neighbouring Czechia, Skoda's Elroq has emerged as one of Europe's most successful electric models. It was the continent's best-selling electric car in July and ranked second over the first seven months of the year, with 67,000 vehicles sold, behind Tesla's Model Y.

Poland's ambitions have been slower to materialise. State-owned ElectroMobility Poland (EMP), which unveiled prototypes of its Izera electric car in 2020 but has yet to manufacture a vehicle, has secured Taiwan's Foxconn as a partner after the electronics manufacturer selected Poland as its European electric vehicle production hub.

EMP plans to begin construction of a factory in Jaworzno in spring 2027 and start serial production towards the end of 2029. Initial capacity is expected to exceed 100,000 vehicles annually, supported by PLN4.5bn (€1.02bn) from Poland's national environmental fund, financed through the EU recovery programme.

Further south, Stellantis's Kragujevac factory in Serbia has been producing electric Fiat Grande Panda vehicles since early 2025 and now manufactures close to 500 cars daily. Cars account for around 16% of Serbian exports, and economist Petar Veselinovic expects the local unit's revenue to exceed €5bn this year.

Slovenia's Renault-owned Revoz plant in Novo Mesto has added production of the electric Dacia Spring alongside the Renault Twingo and is introducing a second shift. China's Great Wall Motor plans to begin assembling its Ora 5 SUV, available in electric, hybrid and petrol versions, near Lovech in Bulgaria in early 2027.
Manufacturing advances faster than demand

Chinese companies are playing an increasingly important role in building the region's electric vehicle supply chain, from BYD and CATL in Hungary to Gotion in Slovakia and Great Wall Motor in Bulgaria.

The expansion reflects China's broader transition away from conventional vehicles. Electric cars, trucks and rail transport are increasingly displacing petrol and diesel consumption in the world's largest automobile market, with Sinopec's research arm expecting Chinese road fuel demand to decline this year.

For Central and Eastern Europe, however, the challenge is no longer simply attracting manufacturers. The region must also develop a domestic market capable of absorbing more of the vehicles rolling off its new production lines.

T&E wants governments attending this year's COP31 climate summit to agree binding electrification targets, arguing that the transition is necessary not only to tackle climate change but also to strengthen energy security.
In Warsaw, Prague and Zagreb, where more than nine out of 10 new cars still have petrol or diesel engines, that argument has yet to translate into a comparable shift in consumer behaviour.

title: CEE builds Europe's electric cars but consumers reluctant to buy them
